tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

112	
113	- Original: the Working Draft bounds it by `Object`. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuples, such as arrays indexed by pairs, and `Object` holds no tuple.

118	
119	- Original: the implementations gave it the empty type `Bottom`, or left it unsolved, and some such compiled calls failed the JVM's verification. The type group's POPL 2019 paper gives such a parameter its bound.

121	  - a parameter declared with two bounds, neither below the other (ledger row 591);
122	  - a parameter that an argument bounds only from above, whose bound names another static parameter (ledger row 612);
123	  - a parameter that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (ledger row 587).

126	**A call written as an argument**
127	
128	- Original: the specification infers a call's static arguments "from the context of the function call". The checker typed each argument of a call without an expected type. So a static argument that only the result mentions took its bound, or the numeral's type where only a numeral fixed it. For example, with `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]` and `takesBox64(b: BoxT[\ZZ64\])`, the checker refused `takesBox64(mk())`.

It types the argument once for each declaration of the enclosing call, with that declaration's parameter type as the expected type. Then it chooses the most specific declaration that this makes applicable. It never passes over a declaration that accepts the call as written. So a reduction's big operator, which the desugaring writes as an argument, takes the reduction's expected type where its instance at its bound does not fit. Walk gives an argument no expected type (`ProjectFortress/tests/XXXInferCallArgumentWalk.fss`).

The reduction then refused its first element. The POPL 2019 paper's rule has no bound to give: such a bound is not a type until the parameter is known.

A generic type that holds the open parameter admits no more than it admits at `Bottom`. A printed type shows the open parameter as `OPEN`: `BoxU[\OPEN\]` for an object `BoxU[\T\]`. 140	- Original: the specification desugars a reduction or a comprehension by the type of its expression: for generators `gs`, `SUM[gs] e` of type `N` calls `SUM[\N\]`, and `<| e | gs |>` of type `List[\E\]` calls `BIG <|[\E\]|>` (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex`). 170	- Original: the Working Draft allows a sum, a difference, a product or a power as a size, and fixes its value once the static parameters are known, but does not say when two such sizes are the same. 228	- Reason: the lexicographic order serves sorting, and a corner outside the bounds on any axis is outside them.
229	
230	**The trivial open range `(:)`**
231	
232	- Original: `(:)` is a range over `Any`. The interpreter's library gave its `truncL`, `truncR`, `every`, `imposeStride` and `atMost` bodies that answer ranges over `ZZ32`: `(:).truncL(3)` was `3#`.
233	- Resolution: the five throw `FailCalled`, through the library's `fail`, with a message that names `(:)`, and so do `(:):s` and `(:)#n`, which call two of them. `(:)` as a whole subscript, `a[:]`, is unchanged.
234	- Reason: each of the five declared types is a range over `Any`. Generics are invariant, so the old bodies' ranges over `ZZ32` broke those types, and the checker refused them.
235	
236	**`SUM` and `PROD`**
237	
238	- Original: `SUM` and `PROD` reduced over `Number`, under the team's comment "Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically". Every sum had the type `Number`, and an empty sum of `RR64` values was the integer 0.
239	- Resolution: each is one generic declaration over the element type's own algebra, which gives its zero or one at that type (`library.md`).
240	- Reason: `Number`'s operators for any number went with the tower, so each reduction uses the element type's own operator.
241	
242	**Vectors and matrices at an element type that is not a number type**
243	
244	- Original: the specification makes a one-dimensional array whose elements are a subtype of `Number` a vector, and a two-dimensional one a matrix (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex`). The interpreter's library followed it: `array1` and `array2` gave a `Vector` or a `Matrix` at every element type below `Number`, and at `Number` and `AnyIntegral` themselves. The library bounds a vector's element type by `{ Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`), which `Number` and `AnyIntegral` do not satisfy. The checker refused the factories' calls of `vector` and `matrix` as ill-formed types.
245	- Resolution: `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64`. At every other element type they give a plain array, also at a user type that extends `Number`. Walk stops at a plain array's `+` and unary `-` with a failed dispatch. Under walk, a `T` inferred from a `ZZ32` value is walk's run-time type `Int`, not `ZZ32`. So `array1` and `array2` with an inferred element type give a plain array, where the specification gives a vector (ledger row 721). Write the static argument to get a vector. The factories choose by a `typecase` over a witness, a value of their result type. A `typecase` over a value of the element type matched a type below a number type, and its `cast` threw `CastError`. `aggregate.tex` still states the rule at `Number`.
246	- Reason: `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not a well-formed type, because `Number` is not within the vector's bound (`Specification/basic/inference.tex`).
247	
248	**Rounding a rational at an infinity or 0/0**
249	
250	- Original: the Working Draft (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, "Rational Numbers") gives `QQ`'s `floor`, `ceiling`, `round` and `truncate` the result type ℤ, and a later paragraph of that section says they return the argument at +∞, −∞ and 0/0, a rational. The interpreter's library returned the argument, and its `round` stopped walk there.
251	- Resolution: these methods and the brackets ⌊ ⌋ and ⌈ ⌉ throw `DivisionByZero` at those three values.
252	- Reason: the declared result type is ℤ, and a division by zero whose result is an integer throws `DivisionByZero` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex`, "Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators").
253	
254	## Loops and reductions are library code
255	
256	**The lifted type of a reduction without an identity**
257	
258	- Original: the interpreter's library lifted the reductions without an identity, such as `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG //`, to the type `AnyMaybe`, which takes no type argument. Such a reduction wraps each element in a `Just` with its `lift`, joins two wrapped elements by its `simpleJoin` of their contents, and answers `Nothing` for no element. Their `simpleJoin` took and answered `Any`, and their `lift` took `Any`, while `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` declared `lift(r:R)`. The team's tests declared their own such reductions with `simpleJoin` at `Any`, and passed `AnyMaybe` to `generate` as its static argument.
259	- Resolution: `AssociativeReduction[\R\]` lifts to `Maybe[\R\]`. Its `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`, and every `lift` takes `R`. A reduction that extends it declares `simpleJoin` at its element type. Under walk, one declared at `Any` or with untyped parameters leaves the abstract `simpleJoin` without a body: walk refuses such a reduction at load, and one with static parameters stops at its first join. A static argument that names the lifted type is `Maybe[\R\]`, as in `h.generate[\Maybe[\(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]\](TestReduction, sing)` in `ProjectFortress/tests/HeapTest.fss`.
260	- Reason: the checker refused the library's declarations at `Any` in 13 places, and `join`'s `if av <- a` cannot bind from `AnyMaybe`, which is not a `Condition`, a generator of zero or one element. `FortressLibrary.fsi` and `Set`'s `Intersection` already wrote these types. The declarations at `Any` had kept some of walk's reductions running while walk gave `Bottom` to a type parameter that a call did not fix. Walk now instantiates such a reduction as "A reduction or a comprehension without static arguments, under walk" says.
261	
262	**A generator's size, the relational predicate and the default index-value pairs**
263	
264	- Original: the interpreter's library declared no size on `Generator`, though three of the library's bodies read the size of a `Generator`. The relational predicate, the condition that `relationalPredicate(r)` makes (`RelationalPredicateCondition`'s `cond` in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`), asks whether `r` holds between each two consecutive elements of its target, a `Generator`; it read a size and indices from 0 off the target. Under walk, `|g|` of a filter, a nest or a mapped filter stopped, and so did the relational predicate on a filter; on an array whose indices start above 0 it read outside the bounds. `Indexed`'s default `indexValuePairs` answered a mapped generator, printed `mapped(...)`, where an `Indexed` is declared. The checker refused these at nine sites.
265	- Resolution: `Generator` has `opr |self|`, a default that counts the elements by running the generator, as `opr IN` searches them. A type with its own size keeps it. The relational predicate is one reduction in the generator's natural order, as the relational reduction of `Generator2` (`efficientImplRelationalDistributiveImpl` in `Library/Generator2.fss`) is. The default pairs are an object over the indexed value, `SimpleIndexValuePairs`, which prints as its elements and is indexed as the value is; a slice of it keeps each pair's index. So two answers change under walk: the relational predicate on a reversed indexed value follows its natural order, and the default pairs of a value indexed from 5 are indexed from 5, not from 0.
266	- Reason: the checker's refusals. A default keeps "only needs to define the generate method" true (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex`). Counting consumes a consumable generator and never ends on an endless one, as every other derived default of `Generator` does.
267	
268	## Specified, but not built
269	
270	**A parameter whose type is left out**
271	
272	- Original: the components chapter (`Specification/basic/components/type-inference.tex`) says that type inference finds every type that a component leaves out. The compiled checker refused a top-level function's or a method's parameter written without a type, and crashed on a local function's. Walk runs such declarations, except a method that implements an abstract declaration, which stops at its first call (ledger row 405).
273	- Resolution: the compiled path refuses every such parameter of a top-level function, a method or a local function, with "Missing parameter type for" and the parameter's name. A `\revision` box in that file and Appendix I say so.
274	- Reason: no text describes that inference. A crash of the checker is no answer, and the refusal already stood at top level.
275

# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress

The team left three forms of Fortress, which disagree in places:

- the specification;
- walk, with the interpreter's library;
- the compiled path, with the compiler's library.

This part lists each change of the revival made for one of two reasons: two of the team's sources contradict each other, or a program failed. Its headings are the points of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", that the changes qualify.

Each resolution is the rule of this tree. Follow it as you follow a decision of the curator, and question it only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Where it changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources", describes the type group, whose later texts most resolutions follow.

If a source of the team's, an old note or your training disagrees with this skill, find the point below. If it is there, follow the skill: it describes the tree. If it is not, do as `SKILL.md`, "When to explore", says.

A note written before the revival, and your training, can be right about the team's walk and out of date here. Three examples: the number types form a tower, fixed-width arithmetic wraps, and walk converts no argument.

## Dispatch is on every argument, at run time

**Overloads that differ in static parameters**

- Original: the Working Draft forbids two declarations of one name whose static parameters differ. The team's later restart of the specification drops it. Neither implementation enforced it, and the checker implements the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which allows them.
- Resolution: such overloads are allowed, and the specification states the paper's model.
- Reason: the implementations and the library already allow such overloads. Enforcing the sentence would refuse about 180 pairs of declarations in the library's apis.

**The return-type rule**

- Original: the type group's 2011 paper asks for the rule on every instance of a generic declaration. The checker tested one instance, so a pair that broke the rule compiled, and its run failed the JVM's verification.
- Resolution: the checker tests every instance.
- Reason: the paper's rule. Such a program now fails at compile time, not at run time.

**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types**

- Original: the No Duplicates Rule refuses two declarations of which each applies to every call that the other applies to (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker counted two functional methods as duplicates only where their `self` parameters stood at the same position. So, in a trait `S`, `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` passed the checker, and the code generator stopped: "apparently malformed overload set not rejected".
- Resolution: the checker refuses two functional methods with equivalent parameter types wherever their `self` parameters stand. Its message is "There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type", with the domain of the declaration that comes first in the source.
- Reason: the rule, and the type group's 2011 paper, by which two declarations that are each more specific than the other are one declaration (`Papers/Types/rules.tick`). A functional method can be viewed as a top-level function (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Method Declarations").

**Walk's choice between a generic and a plain declaration**

- Original: the Working Draft chooses the most specific declaration by the declared parameter types. Walk chose by the order in which the declarations were written.
- Resolution: walk chooses by the declared types.
- Reason: the specification's rule. A program's answer no longer depends on the order of its declarations.

**`fill` and `tabulate`**

- Original: the interpreter's library declared two array methods named `fill`: one takes a value, one a function of the index. For an element type of `Any` or of a function type, both apply and neither is more specific. The checker refused the pair, and walk called a function meant as the value.
- Resolution: the function form is `tabulate` (`library.md`).
- Reason: a second name ends the ambiguity. Scala's `Array.fill` and `Array.tabulate` have the same two meanings.

## Traits and objects, no classes

**The exclusion rule**

- Original: the type group's papers and the checker have the exclusion rule. The Working Draft does not state it, and some of its examples break it.
- Resolution: the specification states the rule. It keeps the examples that break it, marked "Not allowed".
- Reason: without it, the checker's return-type rule lets through programs that die with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`. The later Types chapter states the rule too.

**What a `comprises` clause says**

- Original: four passages of the Working Draft read the clause as a statement about types, and so are false for some programs that it allows. The type group's later Types chapter reads the clause as a statement about values.
- Resolution: every value of the closed trait, the trait that has the clause, is a value of a listed type. A generic trait may extend the closed trait without being listed, if each type that extends it is below a listed type.
- Reason: read by values, the passages hold for those programs.

**A trait's `override`, and object expressions, under walk**

- Original: walk dropped an inherited declaration only where the object itself declared the `override`, so an object below a trait that overrides ran the overridden declaration. Its load check of the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Meet Rule") skipped object expressions: anonymous objects written inside an expression, such as `object extends { A, B } end`.
- Resolution: a trait's `override` declarations override for every type below it. Walk reads what each trait provides by the rule of "What a type provides", below, as its load check does. Walk lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function. It checks the lifted object as it checks an object. Walk checks a trait, object or lifted object with static parameters through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). It does not check a pair of declarations whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. Walk makes no stand-in, and so no Meet Rule check, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where it cannot make the type. The checker still accepts an object expression that breaks the rule (ledger row 570).
- Reason: the traits chapter (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Method Declarations"), and the Meet Rule, which names object expressions.

**An abstract method without a body, and an `override` that overrides nothing, under walk**

- Original: the traits chapter makes both static errors. It asks an object to define a body for the abstract method itself. An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only if the inherited declaration's parameter type is a strict subtype of the `override`'s, so an `override` at equal parameter types overrides nothing. Walk loaded both: a call of the abstract method stopped with an `InterpreterBug`, "has neither body nor def", and the `override` ran. The compiled checker refuses the first and accepts the second (ledger row 653). The compiled checker split a single parameter type through a `comprises` clause, but not the tuple of a method's parameter types, so it refused bodies at `(Ping, Ping)`, `(Ping, Pong)` and `(Pong, Side)` under `(Side, Side)`, with `Side comprises { Ping, Pong }`.
- Resolution: walk refuses at load an object or object expression without static parameters that leaves an inherited abstract method without a body. In every trait, object and object expression, it refuses at load an `override` that overrides nothing, also one at the inherited declaration's own parameter types. It checks a trait, object or object expression with static parameters once, at its declaration, through the stand-in of "A trait's `override`, and object expressions, under walk". There it does not refuse an `override` of an inherited declaration whose parameter types differ from the `override`'s and mention a static parameter with bounds that walk does not read: an object expression's, which walk lifts without the `where` clauses around it, or one of a declaration that extends a type under a `where` clause (ledger row 693). An instance of a generic trait above a declared object is also checked at its static arguments, where equal parameter types count as overridden. So an `override` is not refused where those arguments make its parameter types equal to the inherited declaration's. An object defines an inherited abstract method by a body at its parameter types, or by bodies at narrower parameter types that together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. The traits chapter now says so. Walk refuses the object where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, at a type whose clause walk cannot read, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. A step is one type that the search splits or keeps. Walk also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728). The compiled checker splits the tuple of parameter types in the same way, and stops at the same limits. Where the abstract method or a covering method has static parameters of its own, it does not split, and refuses a cover that needs the split (ledger row 725). `Random` and `QuickCheck` now define the three abstract methods that their objects did not cover. Walk makes no abstract-method check on a generic object (ledger row 665).
- Reason: the chapter's rules. Coverage is the type group's rule of 2012: the compiled checker's, and the Covered rule of Welterweight Fortress (`Papers/Welterweight/static.tick`). The chapter's sentence on functional methods points to abstract functions, whose concrete declarations must "together cover" the abstract one. The library's `Pairs` and the team's test `FileConversion` define abstract methods by such bodies. With any one narrower body allowed, a call outside it stopped walk at run time with "has neither body nor def". Where the search does not settle, walk refuses the object, as the compiled checker and walk's own Meet Rule check refuse.

**What a type provides**

- Original: the traits chapter says that a type provides the method declarations it declares and inherits, and that it does not inherit one that its own `override` declaration overrides or whose parameter types its own declaration repeats. The compiled checker read every declaration of every supertype as provided, and refused the team's `ProjectFortress/tests/disp0.fss`, whose `override` widens a parameter.
- Resolution: both paths read what a type provides as the chapter says. The checker checks that the return type of an overriding declaration is a subtype of the return type of the declaration that it overrides.
- Reason: the specification's rule, which walk follows (above). The team's own test is valid by it.

**A string's `left` and `right`**

- Original: the interpreter's library declared `String`'s getters `left` and `right`, its first and last characters, as `Maybe[\Char\]`, but answered the character itself, so walk printed `a` for `"abc".left`. The specification is silent.
- Resolution: they answer `Just` of the character, and `Nothing` for the empty string, as `List`'s and the ranges' do.
- Reason: the declared type, which the checker enforced by refusing both bodies.

**`self` in a self-typed trait**

- Original: the Working Draft types `self` as the enclosing trait's type, or with a `comprises` clause, as its intersection with the listed types. The checker did the same. So it refused 29 of the library's default bodies that return or pass `self` where the trait's parameter is declared, such as `floor(self): I = self` in `trait Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. Walk ran them. Nothing checked that a type that extends such a trait is an instance of its argument.
- Resolution: the specification defines a self-type parameter. It is a static parameter `X` of a trait `T` whose `comprises` clause is absent or lists only `...`, bounded in one of two ways:
  - by `T` at its own static parameters, as in `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]`;
  - by a trait with a self-type parameter that `T` extends at `X`.

  In `T`'s method bodies, the checker types `self` as `T[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the type `T[\X\]`. The checker refuses a trait, object or object expression that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. For a trait, it checks the type of `self` in that trait's own bodies. Walk is unchanged. A compiled body that returns `self` still fails the JVM's verification when its class loads with the parameter at an object type.
- Reason: the rule makes the 29 bodies well typed, and refuses nothing else in the library. They are the team's minimal complete definitions of its orders, algebra and arrays. Scala asks the same of a class's self type (*Scala Language Specification 2.13*, section 5.1). The signatures keep the trait's type because the POPL 2019 account of overloading compares declared domains, with no type parameter inside an intersection. With the intersection in the signatures, the checker reported 18 false errors of the return-type rule between the `CMP` declarations of `StandardPartialOrder` and `StandardTotalOrder`. The second form of the bound keeps the team's mixins `ContainmentBySubset` and `ContainmentByComparison` valid as written.

**`SYMDIFF` of a many-entry and a one-entry `IntMap`**

- Original: the library's comment says that `SYMDIFF` "returns the key/value mappings contained in exactly one input map". Its body for a many-entry map (`NodeIM`) and a one-entry map (`SingletonIM`) kept only the entry that `seek` found. Under walk `{0,1,2} SYMDIFF {5}` was `{2,5}`, while the reverse order gave `{0,1,2,5}`. A `SYMDIFF` of two many-entry maps that split down to such a pair lost entries in the same way.
- Resolution: the many-entry map is updated at the one-entry map's key. The key is dropped if the map holds it, and added with the one-entry map's value if not. Both orders give the same map.
- Reason: the library's own comment, and the one-entry map's `SYMDIFF`, which already answered so in the other order.

**`UPLUS` of `IntMap`s on a shared key**

- Original: the library's comment says that `UPLUS`, the disjoint union, throws `KeyOverlap` when a key occurs in both maps. Its body for a many-entry map and a one-entry map kept the many-entry map's value on a shared key, while the reverse order threw. So an `IntMap` comprehension or map expression with a repeated key kept one value or threw, by the order of its entries.
- Resolution: a shared key throws `KeyOverlap` in both orders, also between two many-entry maps. So every `IntMap` comprehension or map expression with a repeated key throws, also where the key repeats with the same value. `BIG UPLUS` over maps that share a key throws too.
- Reason: the library's own comment, and the one-entry map's `UPLUS`, which already threw. `Map`'s comprehension throws on every repeated key. The specification throws `KeyOverlap` where a key repeats with a different value (`Specification/basic/expressions/comprehensions.tex`).

## Static parameters

**The bound of a type parameter that has none written**

- Original: the Working Draft bounds it by `Object`. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuples, such as arrays indexed by pairs, and `Object` holds no tuple.
- Resolution: the bound is `Any`. The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over (`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path").
- Reason: the library works only with `Any`.

**A type parameter that a call does not fix**

- Original: the implementations gave it the empty type `Bottom`, or left it unsolved, and some such compiled calls failed the JVM's verification. The type group's POPL 2019 paper gives such a parameter its bound.
- Resolution: it takes its bound on both paths. Under walk, one whose bound names itself stays open, and a big operator without static arguments takes them from its value or its elements (both below). Walk still gives `Bottom` to these:
  - a parameter declared with two bounds, neither below the other (ledger row 591);
  - a parameter that an argument bounds only from above, whose bound names another static parameter (ledger row 612);
  - a parameter that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (ledger row 587).
- Reason: the paper is the type group's latest word on the rule.

**A call written as an argument**

- Original: the specification infers a call's static arguments "from the context of the function call". The checker typed each argument of a call without an expected type. So a static argument that only the result mentions took its bound, or the numeral's type where only a numeral fixed it. For example, with `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]` and `takesBox64(b: BoxT[\ZZ64\])`, the checker refused `takesBox64(mk())`.
- Resolution: if the checker does not accept a call with its arguments so typed, it types each argument that is a call with inferred static arguments again. It types the argument once for each declaration of the enclosing call, with that declaration's parameter type as the expected type. Then it chooses the most specific declaration that this makes applicable. It never passes over a declaration that accepts the call as written. So a reduction's big operator, which the desugaring writes as an argument, takes the reduction's expected type where its instance at its bound does not fit. Walk gives an argument no expected type (`ProjectFortress/tests/XXXInferCallArgumentWalk.fss`).
- Reason: the context of a call written as an argument is the parameter that it is passed to.

**A type parameter whose bound names itself, under walk**

- Original: walk gave such a parameter the empty type `Bottom` where a call did not fix it, as `SUM`'s `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` in `SUM[i <- 1#100] i`. The reduction then refused its first element. The POPL 2019 paper's rule has no bound to give: such a bound is not a type until the parameter is known.
- Resolution: walk leaves the parameter open. Wherever walk checks a value against the open parameter, every value passes. A generic type that holds the open parameter admits no more than it admits at `Bottom`. A printed type shows the open parameter as `OPEN`: `BoxU[\OPEN\]` for an object `BoxU[\T\]`. A reduction now takes its static arguments by the next entry, and leaves such a parameter open only where it has neither a declared type nor an element.
- Reason: an open parameter refuses no value.

**A reduction or a comprehension without static arguments, under walk**

- Original: the specification desugars a reduction or a comprehension by the type of its expression: for generators `gs`, `SUM[gs] e` of type `N` calls `SUM[\N\]`, and `<| e | gs |>` of type `List[\E\]` calls `BIG <|[\E\]|>` (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex`). Walk gave the big operator's static parameters `Bottom`, or left them open where their bound names them. So an empty `SUM` of `RR64` values gave the integer 0, and `Set`'s `BIG UNION` and `BIG INTERSECTION` stopped at their first element. The library left `__bigOperator`'s local function `body(i)` untyped. It declared `IntMap`'s comprehension operator to return an `IntMap[\Val\]`, while its body is a `Comprehension`.
- Resolution: walk instantiates the big operator in this order:
  1. at the declared type of its value: the type of the local variable that it initialises, or the return type of the top-level or local function that returns it, also where it is the last expression of a block that gives that value. A method's return type, a field's or a top-level variable's type, a parameter's type and an assignment do not direct it;
  2. else at the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types; walk collects the elements before it reduces them. Where the join is outside the bound, such as `Number` for `ZZ32` and `RR64` elements of a `SUM`, the parameter stays open, and each `+` runs at its operands' types;
  3. else, with no element, at each parameter's bound, or open where the bound names the parameter.

  The code is `bigOperatorByElements` in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java`. `__bigOperator` declares `body(i: I): L`, and `IntMap`'s operator returns a `Comprehension[\(ZZ64,Val),IntMap[\Val\],AnyCovColl,AnyCovColl\]`. An element that converts to the instantiated type is converted, as at a call. Any other element stops inside `__bigOperator`, with "body param 1". Walk still differs from the specification in three cases:
  - an empty one that no declared type directs leaves `SUM`'s parameter open, and gives the integer 0, whatever its body's type (ledger row 716);
  - a comprehension inside another clause form, a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets such as `BIG CONCAT[ys <- xss] e`, is built at its elements' run-time types where no declared type reaches it (ledger rows 20 and 717);
  - a user big operator declared to return a trait of its own, such as `opr BIG CATOP[\T\](): CatOperator[\T\]`, takes its bound (ledger row 718).

  On the compiled path, the checker takes a plain bound, or the expected type where the reduction's type at that bound does not fit it. It refuses a reduction whose bound names its parameter, such as `SUM`'s and `PROD`'s (ledger row 731).
- Reason: a type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, narrowed by the call's static return type, here the declared type of the value. Walk has no static types, so it reads its elements' run-time types for the type of the expression. At its bound alone, a comprehension is built at `Any`. With `Bottom`, the typed `body(i)` refused the first element.

**A type parameter with two bounds, one a closed trait, in the checker**

- Original: take `T extends { K, R[\T\] }`, with `K comprises { A, B, C }` and `C` not an `R`. The checker replaced `K` in such an intersection by the listed types that the other bound does not exclude, whatever that bound named. It also split a union on the right of a subtype question before it read the bound of a type variable, a static parameter in scope. So `T`'s bound became a union before the checker read it. The call `h(x)` in `g[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: Box[\T\])`, for an `h` with the same bounds, was refused ("is not applicable to an argument of type Box[\T\]"), or stopped the checker ("Applied a substitution to an And and got an Or"). A valid overloading beside it was refused by the return-type rule.
- Resolution: the checker expands a closed trait only against a bound that names no type variable or inference variable, the checker's placeholder for a static argument that it infers. An inference variable below a union takes the whole union as one upper bound. A type variable below a union is also tried through its bound. Such calls compile and run, and a call outside the bounds is refused as not applicable. Two cases still fail:

- Reason: the specification makes such a call applicable at an instance within the bounds (`Specification/basic/inference.tex`). The type group's subtyping algorithm reads no `comprises` clause (`Papers/Types/fig-subtype.tick`). The POPL 2019 paper proves its matching complete only where no union holds a type parameter.

**Sizes on the compiled path**

- Original: the Working Draft has the size parameters `nat` and `int`. The checker crashed on sized declarations, and a sized program did not compile or load. The team's code generator had reserved a slot for a size's run-time descriptor.

- Reason: it completes the team's design, which carries a size as it carries a type argument.

**Arithmetic in a size**

- Original: the Working Draft allows a sum, a difference, a product or a power as a size, and fixes its value once the static parameters are known, but does not say when two such sizes are the same. The checker refused any arithmetic in a size, and counted a static parameter as different from every numeral. The compiled path spelled the expression into the class's name. Walk stopped on a power.
- Resolution: two sizes are the same when they are written alike once each operation on numerals is computed: `2 3` is `6`, and, for static parameters `s0` and `s1`, `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter, or an expression with one in it, is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...`, for a static parameter `b0` and `NatReflect`'s object `N` (below), the arm `N[\0\]` is reachable. The checker checks a computed size against its parameter's kind, as it checks a numeral. It computes a power of 0, 1 or -1 at any exponent, and of another base up to the exponent 4096. It refuses a larger power as outside every kind. The compiled path computes a size when it names a class, so `Box[\2 + 1\]` and `Box[\3\]` are one class; the class loader does not check a size that it computes against its parameter's kind (ledger row 675). Walk computes a power exactly, as the compiled path does. Both compute no power at a negative exponent, which only a static parameter can give, and walk refuses it.
- Reason: the library writes a product in the storage of its matrices, `mem: PrimitiveArray[\T, (s0 s1)\]` in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, and sums in result types. The grammar allows a power in a size. A `nat` or `int` parameter takes an integer, and a power at a negative exponent is no integer, except of 1 and -1. The team's questions and answers in the specification's appendix "Internal Document" (`Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex`) refuse two overloads at `T[\n+1\]` and `T[\0\]`.

**A size known only at run time**

- Original: `NatReflect`'s `reflect` answers a `NatParam`, a trait that the object `N[\nat n\]` extends (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fsi`). The team's clause of `NatParam`, `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]`, was a comment, and the api's comment says that a `NatParam` passed where `N[\n\]` is expected makes `n` a static parameter. The checker refused every such call in the library; walk ran them, binding the size at dispatch.
- Resolution: the clause is restored, and the specification allows a where-clause variable in a listed type. In the checker, a value of such a trait, passed where the listed type is expected, binds the call's `nat` parameter to the value's own size. That size is known to equal only itself: two values passed in one call have two sizes, and the size does not reach a type that names another size. Walk loads the clause and binds each size at dispatch, as before, so it runs such a call. The compiled run waits for the switch-over (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNatOpenRun.fss`).
- Reason: the team's comment, and the library's run-time factories, which pass `reflect`'s value to functions that take `N[\n\]`.

**Comparing pairs and triples**

- Original: the interpreter's library compared pairs and triples lexicographically with `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP` over element types with no bound, under the team's comment "Shouldn't these operators have to extend something? A,B,C?". Walk compared an element only when the elements before it were equal, so `((1,2),3) < ((1,3),0)` and `(1,()) < (2,())` were `true`. A pair whose first elements were unordered, such as a NaN against a float, stopped walk.
- Resolution: each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`, and walk refuses at the call a pair or triple with an element of another type, such as a pair or `()`, whatever the elements before it decide. Walk also refuses a pair whose elements at one position are numbers of two run-time types, such as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)`, which it answered `true`: it takes the element type at their join, which is no partial order (ledger row 511). A pair or triple whose deciding elements are unordered answers `false` to `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`, and `Unordered` to `CMP`. `Reflect`'s `members` is a list in the order the type declares its members, not a set sorted by name: the set compared its triples, which the bound refuses.
- Reason: the checker refused the bodies of the ten operators, five on pairs and five on triples, at 17 sites. The team bounded the range points' comparisons `PCMP` and `SCMP` per element in 2008, and `false` is what `RR64`'s own comparisons answer for a NaN.

## Numbers are siblings, not a tower

**Tower or siblings**

- Original: the interpreter's library nested the number types: `ZZ32` extended `ZZ64`, which extended `ZZ`. The compiler's library had them as siblings. The tower breaks the exclusion rule: `ZZ32` was an `Integral[\ZZ32\]` and, through `ZZ64`, an `Integral[\ZZ64\]`.
- Resolution: the library makes them siblings, as the compiler's library does.
- Reason: the exclusion rule stays (above), so the tower cannot.

**Conversion under walk**

- Original: the Working Draft converts a call's arguments by coercion when that makes the call apply, and the checker does so. Walk converted nothing: its dispatch code held the team's note "TODO add checks for COERCE".
- Resolution: walk converts by coercion at a call, a typed binding and an assignment. `interpreter.md` says how it chooses the coercion.
- Reason: the specification's rule, which the siblings need for every mix of widths.

**Mixed number types in a generic call**

- Original: neither implementation inferred a static argument through a conversion, and the Working Draft's chapter on inference is a heading and two notes. The tower needed no conversion there: a `ZZ32` was a `ZZ64`.
- Resolution: if the arguments of one type parameter mix number types, it takes the narrowest type into which all of them convert. For a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` that is `ZZ64`, and for a `ZZ32` and an `NN32` too. Walk does not apply this rule to the elements of a tuple or varargs argument: it takes their join (ledger row 511). So it refuses `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` ("Comparing pairs and triples").
- Reason: among siblings, only a conversion joins two widths.

- Original: the Working Draft and the compiled path raise `IntegerOverflow` when a fixed-width result does not fit. Walk wrapped the result.
- Resolution: walk raises `IntegerOverflow` too. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's wrapping operators (`library.md`).
- Reason: the specification and the compiled path already agreed.

**Ranges**

- Original: the interpreter's ranges took any integer type. The compiler's library had ranges over `ZZ32` only.
- Resolution: ranges are over `ZZ32` only (`library.md`).
- Reason: a range counts the indices of an array, and a JVM array index is a 32-bit `int`.

**Bounded ranges of rank 2 and 3**

- Original: the interpreter's library named a bounded range of rank 1, `BoundedScalarRange`, and none of rank 2 or 3, whose indices are pairs or triples of `ZZ32`. Its generic range traits, such as `RangeWithExtent[\I\]` in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, compared indices of their type parameter, which declares no comparison. `|#(0,3)|` was 1, and walk stopped on `((0,0)#).every(-1,-1)`.
- Resolution: `BoundedRange2D` and `BoundedRange3D` name them. The range types over `ZZ32` of each rank, in `Library/RangeInternals.fsi`, declare the comparisons `CMP` and `FORWARD_CMP`, and the generic range traits declare them abstract. `#(0,n)` is empty, and a range made by a prefix `#` is declared a `RangeWithExtent`.
- Reason: the checker refused the ranges' declarations at 36 sites, and walk stopped or answered a wrong size. The library's range types of rank 1 gave the design.

**Checking a range of rank 2 or 3 against bounds**

- Original: the interpreter's library checked a range against an array's bounds (`narrowToRange`, through `checkSelection`) with its index type's `<` and `>`, which compare pairs and triples lexicographically. `((0,0):(9,9)).narrowToRange((2,-1):(5,5))` answered `(2,0):(5,5)` and raised no `IndexOutOfBounds`, so an array's range subscript of rank 2 or 3 with a corner outside the bounds on an axis after the first was cut to the bounds, and a subarray read past them.
- Resolution: the check compares corner by corner, by the ranges' own point order `PCMP`, under which one point is below another only if it is below or equal on every axis. The call above raises `IndexOutOfBounds`, as do such subscripts and subarrays. The check is one function for each rank, `checkSelection`, `checkSelection2D` and `checkSelection3D` in `Library/RangeInternals.fss`, and `narrowToRange`'s bodies are declared at the range types over `ZZ32` of each rank.
- Reason: the lexicographic order serves sorting, and a corner outside the bounds on any axis is outside them.

**The trivial open range `(:)`**

- Original: `(:)` is a range over `Any`. The interpreter's library gave its `truncL`, `truncR`, `every`, `imposeStride` and `atMost` bodies that answer ranges over `ZZ32`: `(:).truncL(3)` was `3#`.
- Resolution: the five throw `FailCalled`, through the library's `fail`, with a message that names `(:)`, and so do `(:):s` and `(:)#n`, which call two of them. `(:)` as a whole subscript, `a[:]`, is unchanged.

- Original: `SUM` and `PROD` reduced over `Number`, under the team's comment "Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically". Every sum had the type `Number`, and an empty sum of `RR64` values was the integer 0.

- Reason: `Number`'s operators for any number went with the tower, so each reduction uses the element type's own operator.

- Original: the specification makes a one-dimensional array whose elements are a subtype of `Number` a vector, and a two-dimensional one a matrix (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex`). The library bounds a vector's element type by `{ Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`), which `Number` and `AnyIntegral` do not satisfy. So `array1` and `array2` with an inferred element type give a plain array, where the specification gives a vector (ledger row 721). Write the static argument to get a vector. The factories choose by a `typecase` over a witness, a value of their result type. A `typecase` over a value of the element type matched a type below a number type, and its `cast` threw `CastError`. `aggregate.tex` still states the rule at `Number`.
- Reason: `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not a well-formed type, because `Number` is not within the vector's bound (`Specification/basic/inference.tex`).

- Original: the Working Draft (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, "Rational Numbers") gives `QQ`'s `floor`, `ceiling`, `round` and `truncate` the result type ℤ, and a later paragraph of that section says they return the argument at +∞, −∞ and 0/0, a rational. - Reason: the declared result type is ℤ, and a division by zero whose result is an integer throws `DivisionByZero` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex`, "Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators").

**The lifted type of a reduction without an identity**

- Original: the interpreter's library lifted the reductions without an identity, such as `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG //`, to the type `AnyMaybe`, which takes no type argument. Such a reduction wraps each element in a `Just` with its `lift`, joins two wrapped elements by its `simpleJoin` of their contents, and answers `Nothing` for no element. Their `simpleJoin` took and answered `Any`, and their `lift` took `Any`, while `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` declared `lift(r:R)`. The team's tests declared their own such reductions with `simpleJoin` at `Any`, and passed `AnyMaybe` to `generate` as its static argument.
- Resolution: `AssociativeReduction[\R\]` lifts to `Maybe[\R\]`. Its `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`, and every `lift` takes `R`. A reduction that extends it declares `simpleJoin` at its element type. A static argument that names the lifted type is `Maybe[\R\]`, as in `h.generate[\Maybe[\(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]\](TestReduction, sing)` in `ProjectFortress/tests/HeapTest.fss`.
- Reason: the checker refused the library's declarations at `Any` in 13 places, and `join`'s `if av <- a` cannot bind from `AnyMaybe`, which is not a `Condition`, a generator of zero or one element. `FortressLibrary.fsi` and `Set`'s `Intersection` already wrote these types. - Original: the interpreter's library declared no size on `Generator`, though three of the library's bodies read the size of a `Generator`. The relational predicate is one reduction in the generator's natural order, as the relational reduction of `Generator2` (`efficientImplRelationalDistributiveImpl` in `Library/Generator2.fss`) is. The default pairs are an object over the indexed value, `SimpleIndexValuePairs`, which prints as its elements and is indexed as the value is; a slice of it keeps each pair's index. So two answers change under walk: the relational predicate on a reversed indexed value follows its natural order, and the default pairs of a value indexed from 5 are indexed from 5, not from 0.
- Reason: the checker's refusals. A default keeps "only needs to define the generate method" true (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex`). Counting consumes a consumable generator and never ends on an endless one, as every other derived default of `Generator` does.

**A parameter whose type is left out**

- Original: the components chapter (`Specification/basic/components/type-inference.tex`) says that type inference finds every type that a component leaves out. The compiled checker refused a top-level function's or a method's parameter written without a type, and crashed on a local function's. - Reason: no text describes that inference. A crash of the checker is no answer, and the refusal already stood at top level.

Each landed rung's "Revival change" section, both its parts word for word, in the order the rungs landed, with the rows' numbers in place of the placeholders and W's subsection headings one level down. ### S (`rung-solver-speed`, `ee6bfcb8d`)

**The change.**

- **The team's source.** The team's compiled checker reduced a constraint formula afresh every time it was asked: `Formula.reduce` at `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:356` (528438ac5). - **What the tree now does.** The checker keeps each analyzer's reductions, each exclusion by the question with its inference variables renamed apart, and each table lookup by name. Each memo has a switch, default on. Tests: `ReductionMemoJUTest`, `ExclusionMemoJUTest`, `TraitTableMemoJUTest`.
- **What does not change.** No rule of the language changes: the checker accepts and refuses the same programs, with the same errors at the same places, on the count stage and in every reused answer the audits computed again. The one site that moved, on the distance stage, is row 488's `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:130`, whose presence depends on what the checker asked earlier (F-232); the audit copy of the same code keeps it.

The count stage over the interpreter's library takes about 1.5 minutes (97 s and 83 s on the final code, at loads 3.6 and 3.6), not about 6, and the distance stage about 10 minutes (574 s at load 4.6), not about 18 (1,075 s at climb batch 15b's gate).

The count stage took 437 s before and 97 s after, in one session, with equal tables and whole outputs. 1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time
2	
3	**count stage**
4	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library and prints its errors: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`.
5	
6	The code of this area is in these directories:
7	
8	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
9	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
10	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
11	
12	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
13	
14	## What the two paths share
15	
16	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
17	
18	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
19	- Number natives: walk's `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`), and the compiled `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`).
20	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
21	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
22	
23	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
24	
25	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
26	
27	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
28	
29	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.
30	
31	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
32	
33	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
34	
35	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
36	- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
37	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
38	
39	It also refuses a function, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause or a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).
40	
41	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
42	
43	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
44	
45	## What the code generator does
46	
47	`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.
48	
49	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
50	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
51	- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
52	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time"). If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
53	
54	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:Storage is' 'positions:array design'
55	
56	## The run time
57	
58	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
59	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.
60	
61	## Natives
62	
63	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
64	
65	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.
66	
67	## Traps of the compiled path
68	
69	- Before disambiguation, the compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object`, not `Any`. Walk does not. So the compiled path rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type, until the switch-over (ledger row 412).
70	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
71	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
72	
73	## The `fortress` commands
74	
75	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
76	
77	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
78	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
79	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
80	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.
81	
82	## Running
83	
84	    cd ProjectFortress
85	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
86	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
87	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]
88	
89	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.
90	
91	- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
92	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.
93	
94	## Before an edit
95	
96	Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both date from September 2026, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.
97	
98	- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.
99	
100	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'
101	
102	- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the run time and B.12 the natives.
103	
104	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'
105	
106	- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.
107	
108	## Testing an edit here
109	
110	- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:
111	
112	      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
113	      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
114	      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
115	      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
116	      bin/fortress run P
117	
118	  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
119	- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).
120	
121	## The checker's time
122	
123	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
124	
125	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 6 minutes on an idle machine. It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
126	
127	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
128	
129	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
130	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. A line that differs only in order counts as equal: the order of the apis' checks, or of a union's members in a message. Any other difference fails.
131	
132	The order can move because the checker's output depends on the JVM's identity-hash sequence. Each node's hash starts from its class's identity hash. If any code asks for an identity hash at another moment, hash maps and sets of nodes iterate in another order. An unrelated edit can do this, and so can an instrumented copy.
133	
134	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node, so one long walker method slows the whole checker. `WalkerJUTest` fails if a method of `Walker` grows past the limit: run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=WalkerJUTest`. If it fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`.
135	
136	Two idle runs of one tree differed by about 6 %. So a change is slower if its time is above the base's by more than 6 %.
137	
138	If you change the checker:
139	
140	1. Before each timed run, run `ps aux`. If it shows an `ant` or `java` process of another tree, wait for it to end, for up to 30 minutes. Then take the run anyway, and give the load at its start (`uptime`).
141	2. Before you start, measure the base. In a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), start the count stage in the background (`session.md`). Until it ends, build and run nothing. You may edit.
142	
143	       export W=<your tree> ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
144	       nohup bash -c 's=$(date +%s); explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/base.txt $W/tmp/count/base; rc=$?; echo "seconds $(( $(date +%s) - s ))"; echo EXIT=$rc' > $W/tmp/count-base.log 2>&1 &
145	
146	3. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
147	4. In a call set up for your tree, run the count stage in the same way, named `change`. Take the base and this run with no stop of the process or the VM between them. After such a stop, measure the base again.
148	5. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
149	6. After the second pass, run the count stage again, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. If a line differs only in order, show the diff in your report, and say so of each line. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite").
150	7. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 6. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
151	8. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, and the two comparisons of `change` and `pass`.
152	
153	To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and a scan of the build for methods over 8,000 bytes. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):
154	
155	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'
156	
157	If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself, with step 1 before each run. Run the base from the base build, as step 2 says. Run the worker's commit of step 3 and its head in a worktree seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your change's time moved against your base as the worker's did, within 6 %. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.
